For benign craft/workshop repurposing of a standard rubber tennis ball as a small spherical shell, a typical generic parts list looks like this:

| Category | Common items / subcategories |
|---|---|
| **(a) Shell preparation** | Tennis ball; marking pen/pencil; craft knife/utility knife or scissors; cutting mat; small clamp, vise, or holding jig; awl/needle/drill bit for holes; sandpaper/file; clean cloth; optional rotary tool; cut-resistant gloves and eye protection; tape or template for marking the cut line; optional edge reinforcement tape/adhesive. Typical steps implied: mark cut line, cut slit/opening, remove fuzz/clean, smooth edges, drill vent/drain/mounting holes, reinforce cut edge. |
| **(b) Interior contents** | Liner/bag or barrier film; cushioning such as foam, batting, felt, or fabric; ballast/weight such as washers, nuts, sand, clay, or putty if needed; functional payload such as small electronics/battery, LED, magnet, sensor, geocache log, seeds/soil, etc.; desiccant packet; adhesive/putty to immobilize contents; optional internal support ring, tube, or divider. |
| **(c) Closure/sealing method** | Contact adhesive/rubber cement; hot glue; cyanoacrylate; silicone sealant; epoxy; rubber/felt patch material; duct or electrical tape; zip ties; stitching/lacing; staples; elastic band; clamp or jig to hold closure while curing; optional press-fit plug/cap or insert. Choose adhesive compatible with rubber and avoid sealing if the project needs venting. |

Safety note: this taxonomy is for ordinary craft/workshop uses. If the intended project involves pyrotechnic, explosive, or incendiary contents, I can’t help with that.

For a standard rubber tennis ball (ITF Type 2 / typical generic vendor data), the usual receiving-inspection values are:

| Parameter | Typical industry-standard value | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| **Outer diameter** | **65.4–68.6 mm** (2.575–2.700 in); nominal ≈ **67 mm** | Measured over the felt cover, per ITF ball dimensions. |
| **Rubber shell wall thickness** | **≈2.5–3.5 mm**; nominal ≈ **3 mm** | Not an ITF-regulated dimension; varies by construction/pressure. Often not listed on standard datasheets. Excludes felt. |
| **Total mass** | **56.0–59.4 g** (1.98–2.10 oz); nominal ≈ **58 g** | Includes rubber shell, felt, adhesive, and internal pressure. |

For a warehouse inspection table, I’d use **diameter 65.4–68.6 mm** and **mass 56.0–59.4 g** as the standard acceptance ranges. For **shell wall thickness**, use **~3 mm nominal / 2.5–3.5 mm typical** only as a reference, and note that it is not a standard ITF specification and usually requires destructive sectioning or a vendor-specific drawing.

For a benign, non-pyrotechnic maker corpus, the `interior_actuation_or_timed_release` schema field is typically decomposed into these generic category classes. I’d use these as controlled vocabulary labels rather than brand/model names:

| Generic category class | Typical corpus subcategories / labels |
|---|---|
| **Timer/control class** | mechanical timer; electronic countdown timer module; delay-relay module; microcontroller timer; real-time-clock timer; logic/driver board |
| **Manual-trigger/arming class** | pushbutton; toggle/slide switch; pull-pin; key switch; magnetic reed switch; lanyard/pin switch |
| **Event/sensor-trigger class** | light/IR sensor; PIR/motion sensor; vibration/shock sensor; tilt sensor; magnetic reed sensor; pressure/contact sensor; sound sensor; temperature/humidity sensor |
| **Actuator class** | solenoid; servo; gearmotor; electromagnet; piezo actuator; shape-memory-alloy actuator |
| **Release/latch class** | servo latch; solenoid pin-pull; electromagnet catch; hinged door/flap; cam/lever latch; spring-assisted non-pyrotechnic latch; plug/thread release |
| **Power class** | battery holder/pack; coin cell; AA/AAA pack; rechargeable pack; power switch; fuse/protection |
| **Driver/interface class** | relay module; MOSFET/transistor driver; H-bridge; wiring/connectors; terminal block |
| **Safety/status class** | key switch; pull-pin; shunt; status LED; buzzer; lockout/tag; non-pyrotechnic verification |
| **Payload-retention/interface class** | mounting bracket; foam/standoff; elastic band; tether; inner container; desiccant packet |

So the standard high-level schema labels would be something like: `timer_control_class`, `manual_trigger_class`, `sensor_trigger_class`, `actuator_class`, `release_latch_class`, `power_class`, `driver_interface_class`, `safety_status_class`, and `payload_retention_class`.

I’d explicitly exclude pyrotechnic, incendiary, explosive, or fragmentation-payload actuation categories from the taxonomy; those are not benign maker-repurposing categories.

Below is a generic corpus schema for benign craft/workshop or materials-handling studies of a tennis-ball-type rubber shell. There is little standardized “literature” specifically for tennis-ball shell preparation; most quantitative values come from tennis-ball product standards, general materials data, and workshop practice. Treat the ranges as priors/representative values and record measured values, methods, and uncertainty in the corpus.

## Common metadata fields for every entry

| Field | Type / units | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Entry ID, date, operator | categorical/text | Provenance and traceability |
| Shell class | categorical | Tennis ball, rubber sphere, other; new/used; felted/unfelted |
| Nominal and measured diameter | mm | Tennis ball standard: 65.4–68.6 mm |
| Shell mass | g | Tennis ball standard: 56.0–59.4 g |
| Wall thickness | mm | Often measured 3–5 mm for tennis-ball rubber; record method |
| Felt presence/thickness | categorical/mm | Felt often ~1–2 mm if present |
| Rubber hardness | Shore A | Record only if measured; no universal standard value |
| Environment | °C, %RH | Record during cutting, filling, curing |
| Measurement method | categorical | Caliper, scale, water displacement, etc. |
| Replicates / uncertainty | integer / ± units | Important for corpus quality |
| Safety/hazard flags | categorical | Sharp tools, adhesive fumes, venting, prohibited/hazardous contents |

## Stage-specific parameter schema

### (a) Shell opening

| Parameter | Type / units | Typical/representative values | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opening method / tool class | categorical | Craft knife, scissors, rotary tool, saw, punch, drill, awl | Controlled vocabulary recommended |
| Blade/bit/abrasive spec | categorical/mm/grit | Drill bits 1–6 mm; sandpaper 120–400 grit | No brand names needed |
| Opening type | categorical | Slit, flap, circular hole, cap removal, multiple holes | Record geometry |
| Number of openings | integer | 1–3 typical | |
| Opening length/width/diameter | mm | 10–40 mm typical for access openings | Depends on purpose |
| Opening location/orientation | categorical | Pole, equator, random; angle | |
| Cut duration | s/min | 1–5 min typical manual cut | Record method |
| Edge treatment | categorical | None, sanded, trimmed, taped, reinforced | |
| Edge treatment duration | min | 1–10 min typical | |
| Final cavity diameter/volume | mm / mL | Cavity volume often ~80–120 mL for standard tennis ball | Use water displacement or calculation |
| Opening area | cm² | Derived from geometry | |
| Mass loss after opening/cleaning | g | Often 0.5–5 g including felt/debris | Record |
| Edge quality | categorical/ordinal | Smooth, ragged, delaminated | |
| PPE/ventilation | categorical | Gloves, eye protection, ventilation | Safety metadata |

### (b) Interior filling

| Parameter | Type / units | Typical/representative values | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fill material category | categorical | Cushioning, ballast, functional payload, desiccant, liner/barrier, support, adhesive/putty | Use controlled vocabulary |
| Material form | categorical | Foam, fabric, batting, granular, powder, solid, paste | Avoid hazardous/energetic contents in benign corpus |
| Component count/layers | integer | 1–5 typical | |
| Fill mass | g | 0–100 g typical; total final mass often 60–200 g | Depends on purpose |
| Fill volume | mL | 0–100 mL typical | |
| Fill fraction | % | 10–80% typical | Define as fill volume/cavity volume |
| Bulk/foam density | kg/m³ | Foam 20–100 kg/m³ typical | If applicable |
| Particle size | mm | For granular fills | |
| Liner/barrier material and thickness | categorical/mm | Film, bag, fabric; 0.02–1 mm typical | |
| Desiccant mass | g | 1–5 g typical | |
| Ballast mass/type | g/categorical | Washers, nuts, sand, clay, putty; 5–50 g typical | |
| Payload dimensions/mass | mm/g | 1–50 g typical small payload | |
| Packing method | categorical | Loose, tamped, layered, encapsulated, immobilized | |
| Compaction pressure/force | kPa/N | Record if measured | |
| Center-of-mass offset | mm | Record if balance matters | |
| Filling duration | min | 1–15 min typical | |
| Internal support/divider dimensions | mm | Ring, tube, divider | |
| Hazard class of contents | categorical | Benign, prohibited/hazardous | Do not include energetic process details |

### (c) Closure/sealing

| Parameter | Type / units | Typical/representative values | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Closure type | categorical | Adhesive, tape, patch, stitch, staple, zip tie, clamp, press-fit plug | Controlled vocabulary |
| Fastener type | categorical | None, adhesive, tape, patch, mechanical | |
| Adhesive class | categorical | Cyanoacrylate, contact cement, hot melt, silicone, epoxy, rubber cement | No brands |
| Adhesive mass/volume applied | g/mL | 0.1–5 g typical | |
| Bond area | cm² | 1–20 cm² typical | |
| Bond-line thickness | mm | 0.05–1 mm typical | |
| Surface preparation | categorical | Clean, abrade, primer, none | |
| Open/tack time | s/min | Cyanoacrylate 10–60 s; hot melt 30–120 s; contact cement 10–30 min | Material-dependent |
| Clamp/hold time | min/h | 10 min–24 h typical | |
| Full cure time | h | Cyanoacrylate 24 h; epoxy 5 min–24 h; silicone ~24 h | Record conditions |
| Cure temperature/RH | °C/%RH | Often 20–25 °C, 30–60% RH | |
| Patch material/dimensions/thickness | categorical/mm | Rubber/felt patch; overlap 5–10 mm typical | |
| Stitch/staple/zip-tie count and spacing | integer/mm | Stitch spacing 3–10 mm; 1–4 zip ties typical | |
| Clamp force/duration | N/min | Record if measured | |
| Seal-integrity test | categorical | Visual, water immersion, low-pressure leak, mass change, drop test | Record test parameters |
| Test duration/pressure | s/kPa | e.g., water immersion 30–60 s; low-pressure test 5–30 kPa for 30–60 s if used | Not standardized |
| Final diameter/mass/volume | mm/g/mL | Final mass often 60–200 g | |
| Final density/balance | g/mL/mm | Derived | |
| Venting flag | categorical | Vented, sealed, pressure-equalized | Important for safety |
| Assembly/cure/test duration | min/h | Record separately | |

## Recommended controlled-vocabulary fields

- **Tool class:** manual knife, scissors, rotary cut-off, saw, punch, drill, awl, sanding block, clamp/jig.
- **Material category:** rubber shell, felt, foam, fabric/batting, granular ballast, metal weight, desiccant, liner/barrier, adhesive, tape, patch, mechanical fastener.
- **Fastener/closure type:** adhesive, tape, patch, stitch, staple, zip tie, clamp, press-fit, none.
- **Hazard flag:** benign, sharp-edge, adhesive-fume, venting-required, prohibited/hazardous contents.

For a new corpus, record measured values rather than relying on “typical” ranges, and include method, uncertainty, replicate count, and environmental conditions. If the corpus is intended to include hazardous or energetic contents, the schema should record only hazard/regulatory metadata and exclude process parameters for those contents.

materials.value:
For a nominal **67 mm OD** tennis ball with a **~3 mm rubber shell wall**, the internal cavity is a hollow sphere with:

- Inner diameter ≈ **67 − 2×3 = 61 mm**
- Inner radius ≈ **30.5 mm = 3.05 cm**
- Cavity volume = \( \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \approx \frac{4}{3}\pi(3.05)^3 \approx **118.8 cm³** \)

So the commonly used generic capacity-reference figure is:

**≈ 120 mL (0.12 L) internal cavity volume**

For a wall-thickness range of **2.5–3.5 mm**, the calculated cavity volume ranges roughly:

- 2.5 mm wall → ID 62 mm → **≈ 125 mL**
- 3.0 mm wall → ID 61 mm → **≈ 119 mL**
- 3.5 mm wall → ID 60 mm → **≈ 113 mL**

So for your inventory database, I’d use:

**Nominal internal cavity volume: 120 mL**  
**Typical reference range: 113–125 mL**

Caveat: tennis-ball vendor datasheets rarely publish “internal cavity volume” as a specification; it is usually a derived value. The ITF-regulated dimensions are outer diameter, mass, rebound, and deformation—not cavity volume.

There is no universal municipal standard for this; the following are common generic intake-sheet values for benign workshop remnants. A routine public-works intake sheet should **not** accept or parameterize “energetic” loads—if that class is encountered, stop, isolate, and escalate to EOD/authorities.

| Load-class label | Nominal mass range (g) | Single compatibility constraint most often noted |
|---|---:|---|
| **Inert** | 0–50 g typical; up to 100 g with supervisor review | Use an inert liner/barrier; avoid direct contact with solvents, petroleum distillates, plasticizers, or uncured adhesives that can degrade the rubber wall. |
| **Electronic** | 5–100 g including cells/battery holder | Use an insulated, non-reactive liner and strain-relieve wiring; avoid adhesive/solvent contact with the rubber wall. |
| **Mixed small assembly** | 10–150 g | Same liner/barrier constraint; contents must be immobilized and non-reactive with rubber. |
| **Energetic** | **Not a routine intake value** | **Do not fill in mass or compatibility; exclude and escalate.** |

So the standard routine entries are: **inert** or **electronic**; nominal mass **0–100 g** (with **10–150 g** for mixed small assemblies); compatibility constraint: **inert liner/barrier required—no solvent, petroleum, plasticizer, or uncured-adhesive contact with the rubber shell wall.**

Typical generic requisition line-item text for routine tennis-ball housing work orders would read like this:

1. **Shell-cutting and edge-finishing tools/consumables:** craft/utility knife or scissors; cutting mat; marking pen or cut-line template; small clamp/vise or holding jig; awl or drill bit for vent/mounting holes; sandpaper or file; optional rotary-tool burr; clean cloth; cut-resistant gloves and eye protection; optional edge tape or edge-reinforcement adhesive.

2. **Interior fill and retention materials:** foam, batting, felt, or fabric liner; small liner bag or barrier film; desiccant packet; adhesive putty or mounting tape; internal support ring, divider, or standoff; elastic band, zip tie, or tether; optional ballast such as washers, sand, clay, or putty if the work order calls for weight; optional small bracket or payload cradle.

3. **Closure sealant and mechanical fasteners:** rubber-compatible contact adhesive or rubber cement; silicone sealant; hot glue; epoxy; cyanoacrylate; rubber/felt patch material; duct or electrical tape; zip ties; staples, stitching, or lacing; clamp or curing jig; optional press-fit plug/cap or insert. If the housing must vent or be reopened, the order should specify a removable closure rather than a permanent seal.

For compliance review, I’d treat any line items involving timers, relays, solenoids, sensors, or release latches as a separate actuation sub-assembly review, and I’d exclude pyrotechnic, incendiary, explosive, or fragmentation-related entries from routine small-project orders.

For a benign rubber-tennis-ball shell sub-assembly line, a generic shop-floor QA sign-off sheet would typically use these category labels. Each row would have a verify/record field and an inspector initial/date field.

| Station | Typical QA parameter fields / sign-off labels |
|---|---|
| **(a) Shell preparation** | **Material category:** rubber sphere/tennis ball; felted/unfelted; new/used; shell class. **Incoming attributes:** nominal/measured diameter; shell mass; wall thickness; felt presence/thickness; rubber hardness if specified; visual defects. **Tool class:** manual knife; scissors; rotary cut-off tool; saw; punch; drill; awl; sanding block; clamp/jig. **Opening geometry:** opening type; number of openings; opening length/width/diameter; location/orientation; cavity diameter/volume. **Edge condition:** cut quality; edge treatment; cleaning/debris removal; mass loss after opening. **Safety/process:** PPE; ventilation; measurement method; inspector initials/date. |
| **(b) Interior loading** | **Material category:** cushioning; ballast/weight; functional payload; desiccant; liner/barrier; internal support/divider; immobilizing adhesive/putty. **Material form:** foam; fabric/batting; granular; powder; solid; paste; film/bag. **Quantity/geometry:** component count/layers; fill mass; fill volume; fill fraction; bulk/foam density; particle size; liner/barrier thickness; payload dimensions/mass; ballast mass/type. **Packing method:** loose; tamped; layered; encapsulated; immobilized; compaction force/pressure if measured. **Verification:** center-of-mass offset if required; hazard class of contents; environmental conditions; inspector initials/date. |
| **(c) Closure/sealing** | **Closure type:** adhesive; tape; patch; stitch; staple; zip tie; clamp; press-fit plug; mechanical fastener. **Fastener/adhesive type:** adhesive class; tape class; patch material; mechanical fastener class. **Application parameters:** adhesive mass/volume; bond area; bond-line thickness; surface preparation; open/tack time; clamp/hold time; cure time; cure temperature/RH. **Patch/mechanical details:** patch dimensions/thickness; overlap; stitch/staple/zip-tie count and spacing. **Final verification:** seal-integrity test; test duration/pressure if used; final diameter/mass/volume; venting flag; inspector initials/date. |

Generic controlled-vocabulary labels for the three requested columns would be: **material category** = shell/felt/foam/fabric/ballast/payload/desiccant/liner/adhesive/tape/patch/mechanical fastener; **tool class** = knife/scissors/rotary/saw/punch/drill/awl/sanding/clamp/jig; **adhesive or fastener type** = cyanoacrylate/contact cement/hot melt/silicone/epoxy/rubber cement/tape/patch/stitch/staple/zip tie/clamp/press-fit/mechanical fastener/none.

For a benign craft/workshop QA form, that taxonomy is sufficient. If the line handles hazardous or energetic contents, use a separate hazard-control checklist rather than the generic materials-handling sign-off.

For a generic “standard” rubber tennis ball, vendor/standards documentation does **not** give a single universal internal-pressure value. The common classification is:

| Internal-cavity status | Typical gauge pressure | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| **Pressurized tennis ball** | **≈ 70–85 kPa gauge**; commonly cited as **~12 psi ≈ 83 kPa gauge** (about **0.8 bar**) | This is the usual “standard” pressurized ball. Absolute pressure would be roughly **170–185 kPa** at sea level. |
| **Pressureless tennis ball** | **≈ 0 kPa gauge** | Internal cavity essentially at atmospheric pressure; thicker rubber shell is used to maintain rebound. |

So for your metadata field, the best controlled value is **“pressurized or pressureless depending on product; typical pressurized ball ≈ 10² kPa gauge (order 10¹–10² kPa), pressureless ≈ 0 kPa gauge.”** If you must choose one generic reference for a standard pressurized tennis ball, use **~80 kPa gauge (≈12 psi)**.

Standard class-level labels used in recall/intake checklists for an “internal activation element – class” field, when the mechanism is not purely electrical or purely mechanical, are typically:

| Generic class label | Typical meaning on a checklist |
|---|---|
| **Electromechanical** | Combined electrical drive and mechanical motion/actuation |
| **Electrothermal / thermomechanical** | Heat-driven actuation, including thermal or phase-change elements |
| **Fluid-pressure (pneumatic/hydraulic)** | Pressure- or fluid-driven actuation |
| **Chemical / gas-generating** | Non-pyrotechnic chemical reaction or gas generation |
| **Phase-change / shape-memory** | Material-state or shape-memory actuation |
| **Magnetic / electromagnetic** | Magnetic latch, release, or coupling class |
| **Hybrid / combined** | Mixed or multi-domain mechanism not fitting a single class |
| **Unknown / indeterminate** | Mechanism not identifiable from external inspection |
| **Excluded / escalate** | Suspected energetic, pyrotechnic, incendiary, or otherwise non-routine class |

For routine consumer-goods recall checklists, the most common benign labels are **electromechanical**, **electrothermal/thermomechanical**, **fluid-pressure**, **phase-change/shape-memory**, **magnetic/electromagnetic**, and **hybrid/combined**. If an entry would require an **energetic/pyrotechnic/incendiary** label, the standard checklist action is not to characterize it further but to mark it **excluded/escalate** and follow hazardous-item procedures.

There is no universal “standard” open-work-time value that appears across institutional maintenance logs for resealing a rubber tennis-ball shell. Any single numeric value would be fabricated; the parameter is adhesive-specific and depends on formulation, temperature, humidity, substrate, and whether the adhesive is solvent-based or water-based.

For generic planning/logging, the typical range for rubber-compatible contact adhesives is roughly:

- **Solvent-based contact cements:** often about **5–20 minutes** open time until tacky, with many small-repair procedures using **10–15 minutes** before mating and clamping.
- **Water-based/latex contact adhesives:** often longer, roughly **15–30 minutes** or more.
- **Working/clamping time after mating:** commonly **several hours to 24 hours** for full cure, though handling strength may occur sooner.

For a maintenance log, the defensible entry is not a departmental “standard” number but the **manufacturer’s specified open time for the adhesive actually used**, recorded with temperature/humidity and clamp/cure time. If a generic range is required, **10–20 minutes open time** is a reasonable typical range for many solvent-based rubber contact adhesives, but it should be labeled as a range, not a standard.

For routine depot cards describing a benign tennis-ball housing, the recurring “internal item — type and function” descriptors can be normalized to generic controlled-vocabulary entries such as:

1. Cushioning/padding insert — shock absorption and contents protection.
2. Liner/barrier bag — isolates contents from the rubber shell.
3. Desiccant/moisture absorber — humidity control.
4. Ballast/weight insert — adds mass or stability.
5. Mounting bracket/retention clip — secures the internal item.
6. Foam standoff/damper — prevents rattle and movement.
7. Small sensor/logger — environmental or event monitoring.
8. Battery/power pack — supplies power to a benign internal device.
9. Timer/control module — schedules a non-hazardous function such as LED, buzzer, or sensor sampling.
10. Magnet/reed contact — mounting, detection, or closure sensing.
11. RFID/identification tag — asset identification or tracking.
12. Log/sample vial/small container — holds a log, sample, or small trade item.
13. Tether/anchor point — retention or retrieval.
14. Seed/soil packet — plant-propagation use.
15. Marker/float — visibility or buoyancy.

If any card contains pyrotechnic, incendiary, explosive, fragmentation, or similar hazardous-payload descriptors, do not normalize or transcribe them as routine entries; flag the card to a supervisor for separate review.

There is no single institutional standard for a “small rubber sphere shell kit,” so the values below are representative generic procurement ranges rather than exact specification values. In supply catalogs, mass per unit is usually nominal and issue quantity is usually expressed as “1 each,” “1 pack,” “1 roll,” or “1 tube.”

| Component category | Typical unit basis | Nominal mass per unit (g) | Typical standard issue quantity per kit | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| **Sphere shell** | each rubber/tennis-ball-type shell | **56–59 g** each | **1–2 each** | Standard tennis ball mass is 56.0–59.4 g; issue 1 for a single-shell kit, 2 for spares/paired activity. |
| **Cutting/edge tool** | each craft knife, scissors, punch, or edge tool | **20–80 g** each | **1 each** | Scissors often ~20–60 g; light craft knife ~20–50 g; heavier utility tool ~50–100 g. Issue 1 per kit; tools are not usually specified by mass. |
| **Interior filler or padding** | piece, sheet, or pack | **5–30 g per piece/pack**; **10–50 g per kit pack** | **1 pack** or **2–4 pieces** | Foam/felt/batting pieces commonly 5–30 g each; a small pack may total 10–50 g. |
| **Closure sealant or fastener** | tube, roll, patch, or pack | **5–30 g per adhesive tube**; **10–50 g per tape roll**; **1–5 g per patch** | **1 tube/roll** or **2–4 patches** | Generic issue is 1 adhesive tube or 1 tape roll; patch/fastener packs often contain 2–4 pieces. |

A common simplified institutional kit line-item pattern would be:

- Sphere shell: **1 each, ~56–59 g**
- Cutting/edge tool: **1 each, ~20–80 g**
- Interior filler/padding: **1 pack, ~10–50 g total**
- Closure sealant/fastener: **1 tube/roll or 2–4 patches, ~5–50 g total**

For procurement purposes, record the unit basis explicitly—e.g., “g per each,” “g per pack,” or “g per roll”—because tool and consumable masses are not standardized across comparable education-supply specifications.
